newsitem.title: HUNGARY: East European markets share worldwide nervousness.
newsitem.headline: East European markets share worldwide nervousness.

text.p: Central and eastern European share markets mostly fell sharply this week as Wall Street, which hit a record high on Tuesday, gave little help to the region's bourses.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which follows price movements in 73 Czech, Polish, Hungarian, Slovak and Slovenian stocks, shed almost two percent.
BUDAPEST
The Hungarian share market tumbled nearly five percent this week and traders, although divided on how long the sluggish period would last, said they expected the underlying trend to remain unchanged.
Many traders believe that a sideways trend will last until the next phase of the privatisation of oil company MOL in May, but there are who believe that falling prices may encourage new purchases.
"I'm not that pessimistic," said Andrea Keresztesi of ABN-AMRO Hoare Govett (Hungary) said. "Should the market fall some more it would become attractive again and trigger some rises."
On Thursday the BUX index closed at 5,118.60 points, down 262.55 from last Friday.
WARSAW

Polish shares fell 1.6 percent this week and analysts said the market, now at 17,414.8 points on the WIG index, would apparently fall more after having gained 38 percent from mid-December to mid-February.

"There's been no radical overvaluing for us to expect a big correction...but definitely we'll have a correction of about 10 percent to 16,000 points," said Michal Szczurek, an analyst at ING BSK Asset Management.
Other analysts said 17,000 points would more likely provide support. Analysts said small-cap stocks, the recent leaders, had joined blue chips in performing poorly.
PRAGUE

Czech shares moved lower throughout the week with analysts saying foreign investors were becoming increasingly cautious about prospects for Czech equities because of concerns about the country's macroeconomic fundamentals.
"Generally it (the downturn) is caused by lack of demand because there are no new orders from abroad and domestic speculators see no reason to buy," said Pavel Sobisek of Zivnostenska Banka.
"People are just sitting and watching," added Radim Bajgar of ING Barings.
The three most heavily capitalised shares on the PX50 -- SPT Telecom, CEZ and Komercni Banka -- which account for 45 percent of the index's capitalisation dropped by an average of 3.6 percent.
BRATISLAVA
The Slovak bourse extended its mini bull run of the past few weeks with the official 16-share SAX index reaching a year high of 207.75 points on Tuesday.

Brokers said the Slovak bourse appeared unaffected by the current downtrend on the neigbouring markets, adding that the BSE should hold at its current levels, or post a slight increase, in the mid-term.
"Even after including the potential risk of the political situation, our market is still undervalued compared with other bourses in the region," said Libor Briska of Creditanstalt.
On Thursday the SAX index finished at 206.38 points, down a fraction from last Friday.
ZAGREB

Croatian stocks were mixed on lower volumes on Thursday, but traders said the lull was only temporary as the market geared up for further gains. The lull came about as investors became cautious, awaiting results of the local elections set for April 13.
Traders singled out fully-listed Zagrebacka Banka as the most promising issue, which will set the pace for the rest of the market. The bank hit an all-time high on Wednesday.
"Zagrebacka is going sky-high, but we feel there is quite some potential left for further growth," Damir Cikotic of Faktor brokerage said.
LJUBLJANA

Slovenian shares firmed 1.35 percent this week, pushing the SBI index to 1,396.34 points, up 18.64. Brokerage Dadas sharply outperformed the market, soaring more than 32 percent. Turnover on the Slovenian bourse's primary market totalled $1.96 million.
BUCHAREST
Bucharest bourse turnover edged lower with most stocks falling this week as investor interest continued to dim.
Trading at the week's three sessions was dominated by first-tier Oltchim SA chemical plant and fertiliser maker Azomures SA, with interest in second-tier shares almost absent.
Brokers said several factors, including a firmer leu and high interest rates on banking deposits, combined to cap buying by domestic and foreign investors.
